rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Work (W = Fd cos θ for constant force, W = ∫F dx for variable force) is the transfer of energy by a force. The work-energy theorem (W_net = ΔK) connects forces to motion. Gravity (conservative) and friction (non-conservative) are the two most important forces in work problems. Spring work (W = ½kx²) is a standard NEB topic.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Work by constant force: W = Fd cos θ (positive when θ < 90°, negative when θ > 90°, zero when θ = 90°)
Work by variable force: W = ∫ F(x) dx (area under F-x graph)
Work-energy theorem: W_net = ΔK = ½mv² − ½mu²

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ 'Work and energy are different concepts.' ✅ Work is a TRANSFER of energy. When you do work on a body, you transfer energy to it. The work-energy theorem (W_net = ΔK) makes this precise.  ·  ❌ 'Work is a vector because force and displacement are vectors.' ✅ Work is a SCALAR — it is the dot product of force and displacement (W = F·d·cos θ). It has magnitude but no direction.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Work is a scalar — it has magnitude but no direction. Do not assign a direction to work.  ·  The angle θ in W = Fd cos θ is the angle between the force and displacement vectors.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Constant force: A 20 N force pushes a block 5 m at 30° to the horizontal. W = 20 × 5 × cos 30° = 86.6 J.  ·  Variable force (spring): A spring (k = 100 N/m) is stretched from 0 to 0.2 m. W = ½ × 100 × 0.2² = 2 J.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'If a body moves, work must be done.' ✅ Work is done only if the force has a component along the displacement. Centripetal force does zero work in circular motion (always perpendicular to velocity).  ·  ❌ 'Work done by gravity depends on the path.' ✅ Gravity is a conservative force — work depends only on the vertical displacement (mgΔh), not on the path taken.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Solve 5 constant-force work problems (W = Fd cos θ) for different angles.  ·  Solve 5 work-energy theorem problems finding final speed from net work.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Perpendicular shortcut: if force ⊥ displacement, W = 0 — no calculation needed.  ·  Gravity shortcut: W_g = mgΔh — only the vertical displacement matters, not the path.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: A 30 N force pushes a block 10 m at 60° to the horizontal. Find the work done.  ·  A spring (k = 200 N/m) is compressed from 0.1 m to 0.3 m. Find the work done by the spring.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Constant-force work (W = Fd cos θ) is the most common problem type.  ·  Work-energy theorem problems: find the net work and equate to ΔK.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Work is the dot product of force and displacement: W = Fd cos θ — a scalar quantity measured in joules.  ·  The work-energy theorem: W_net = ΔK = ½mv² − ½mu² — connects forces to motion.  ·  Gravity is a conservative force — work depends only on vertical displacement (mgΔh).  ·  Friction is a non-conservative force — work depends on the path length and is always negative.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Work is a scalar — the dot product of force and displacement (W = Fd cos θ).  ·  Work is positive when the force helps motion, negative when it opposes motion, zero when perpendicular.  ·  The work-energy theorem (W_net = ΔK) connects forces to motion — one of the most powerful results in mechanics.  ·  Gravity is conservative — work depends only on vertical displacement, not on the path.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Work is the dot product of force and displacement — a scalar quantity measured in joules.  ·  The work-energy theorem (W_net = ΔK) connects forces to motion and is one of the most powerful results in mechanics.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: A 5 kg block accelerates from 2 m/s to 8 m/s. Find the net work done.  ·  A 3 kg object is lifted 15 m vertically. Find the work done by gravity.  ·  A body moves in a vertical circle of radius 2 m at constant speed 4 m/s. Find the work done by the centripetal force in one complete revolution.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Spring work problems: W = ½kx² — know the formula and when to use it.  ·  Zero-work identification: force perpendicular to displacement, no displacement, no force.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Work-energy theorem: A 2 kg block accelerates from 3 m/s to 7 m/s. W_net = ½ × 2 × (49 − 9) = 40 J.  ·  Gravity: A 5 kg object falls 10 m. W_g = 5 × 9.8 × 10 = 490 J (positive, body speeds up).

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Work done by a constant force:** $W = Fd \cos \theta$, where $F$ is the magnitude of the force, $d$ is the displacement, and $\theta$ is the angle between the force and displacement vectors. Work is a scalar quantity (SI unit: joule, $J = N\cdot m$).…  ·  **Work done by a variable force:** when force varies with position, work is the area under the $F-x$ graph, or mathematically, $W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F(x) \, dx$. For a spring force $F = -kx$, the work done by the spring when stretched from $x_1$ to $x_2$ is $W = \frac{1}{2}k(x_1^2 - x_2^2)$.  ·  **Work-energy theorem:** the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy: $W_{net} = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{1}{2}mu^2$. This is one of the most powerful results in mechanics — it connects forces (through work) to motion (through kinetic energy).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: A spring stores elastic potential energy U = ½kx² — this energy is fully recoverable.  ·  Concept 1: Core definition of Work-Energy Theorem  ·  Concept 2: Key theorem or principle in Work-Energy Theorem

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Work by gravity: W_g = mgΔh = mg(h_i − h_f) (path-independent)  ·  Work by spring: W = ½k(x_i² − x_f²) (spring force F = −kx)  ·  Application formula for Work-Energy Theorem

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Derivation result for Work-Energy Theorem  ·  Friction is non-conservative — work depends on the path length and is always negative (for kinetic friction).  ·  ❌ 'A spring does work W = ½kx² when stretched by x.' ✅ The work done ON the spring to stretch it is ½kx². The work done BY the spring when it returns is also ½kx² (energy is recovered).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ 'Friction always does negative work.' ✅ Static friction can do positive work — e.g., the static friction on your feet pushes you forward when walking. Kinetic friction always does negative work.  ·  Carefully distinguish between similar-looking concepts in work-energy theorem.  ·  Pay attention to the conditions under which formulas and theorems apply.
